bullets: Stave 1: works in a cold ‘dismal little cell’ with a fire ‘so very much smaller that it looked like one coal’; warms himself at the candle: **exploitation**.
He slides down Cornhill twenty times ‘in honour of its being Christmas Eve’: childlike joy despite poverty.
Stave 3: proposes a toast to ‘Mr Scrooge, the Founder of the Feast!’ despite Mrs Cratchit’s anger: **forgiveness and generosity** of spirit.
Stave 4: grieves for Tiny Tim, ‘My little, little child!’; the repetition shows overwhelming love.
Stave 5: arrives late; Scrooge pretends to be angry, then raises his salary: **cyclical** reversal of Stave 1.
Symbolises the **respectable working poor**: hardworking, honest, loving, but trapped by low wages.
core.p: Scrooge’s clerk, paid fifteen shillings a week, supporting a large family.

bullets: ‘God bless us every one!’: **innocence** and inclusive Christian charity; also the novella’s last words.
He hopes people in church will see him and remember ‘who made lame beggars walk, and blind men see’: links to Christ’s compassion.
Ghost of Christmas Present: ‘If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future, the child will die.’
Stave 4: his empty stool and crutch ‘carefully preserved’: **pathos** through absence.
Stave 5: ‘who did NOT die’: capitals emphasise the power of Scrooge’s change.
Symbolises the **vulnerable poor child**; his fate measures society’s compassion.

callouts.p: Dickens makes Tiny Tim deliberately lovable so that Malthus’s ‘surplus population’ becomes a real child the reader cannot bear to lose.

core.p: Bob’s youngest son, who is disabled and ill (‘he bore a little crutch, and had his limbs supported by an iron frame’).

bullets: The Christmas dinner (Stave 3) is small but celebrated as a triumph: ‘There never was such a goose.’
The pudding: ‘a small pudding for a large family’, yet ‘nobody said or thought’ that: contentment.
Mrs Cratchit calls Scrooge ‘odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling’: voices the reader’s anger.
Family love and togetherness contrast with Scrooge’s isolation.
core.p: Mrs Cratchit, Martha, Belinda, Peter and the two younger children.

model: Context: low wages, child mortality, Dickens’s family background
exam.q: Explain how Dickens presents the Cratchit family elsewhere in the novella. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Contrast the Cratchits’ warmth with Scrooge’s isolation.

mistakes.r: He is hardworking and loyal; his position reflects low wages, not his character.
He dies only in the vision of the future; after Scrooge changes, he lives.

quotes.a: Stark warning; ties fate to Scrooge.

summary: Bob Cratchit and Tiny Tim represent the deserving, loving poor: Bob is a loyal, underpaid clerk who still celebrates Christmas joyfully, and Tiny Tim is a disabled child whose survival depends on Scrooge’s change; learn their key moments and what they symbolise.

terms.d: Deliberately emotional writing to move the reader.
